title: Introduction to Python
text:
Control Structures
Python supports the usual logical conditions from mathematics:

# Equals: a == b
# Not Equals: a != b
# Less than: a < b
# Less than or equal to: a <= b
# Greater than: a > b
# Greater than or equal to: a >= b

These conditions can be used in several ways, most commonly in ‘if statements’ and loops.

# if statement:
if 5 > 2:
    print('Five is greater than two!')

title: Introduction to Python
text:
Functions
A function is a block of code which only runs when it is called.
You can pass data, known as parameters, into a function.
A function can return data as a result.

# Defining a function:
def my_function():
    print('Hello from a function')

# Calling a function:
my_function()

title: Exploring Socioeconomic Factors Associated with Low Food Access Tracts in New York State
text:
In the United States, reliable access to affordable, nutritious, and healthy food remains one of the most significant public health and public policy concerns. Today, food accessibility affects not only individual health outcomes but also broader issues related to economic opportunity, public/nonpublic transportation, housing inequality, and poverty. While many communities have access to nearby food sellers, the quality of the food is not up to par. Affordable, healthy food is not equally distributed across neighborhoods. In many urban areas, residents primarily rely on corner stores, delis, and convenience stores rather than grocery stores or supermarkets that offer fresh produce and affordable, healthy food options. Meanwhile, in rural communities, residents often face long distances to food sources. Together, these conditions contribute to what the United States Department of Agriculture now refers to as low-food-access communities, or “food deserts.”
According to the New York State Council on Hunger and Food Policy (2025), food insecurity continues to affect vulnerable populations throughout the state despite ongoing food assistance programs and policy initiatives. Rising food costs, transportation barriers, housing instability, and economic inequality continue to limit many households’ ability to consistently access healthy and affordable food. Unfortunately, according to the New York State Council on Hunger and Food Policy (2025), food insecurity and accessibility issues continue to affect several vulnerable populations throughout New York State. Despite all of the ongoing policy changes and food assistance programs. Housing instability, transportation barriers, economic inequality, and rising food costs, combined with distance to stores, tend to limit many communities’ and households’ ability to consistently access healthy and affordable food.
The motivation for this project comes from the broader importance of understanding how food accessibility affects everyday life within neighborhoods and communities. It affects workers, families, children, and elderly residents, able-bodied and non-able-bodied alike. All throughout rural and urban New York State. That being said, there is hope. For instance, data like ours helps identify which communities and neighborhoods face the most food access challenges. Then, policymakers, local governments, community organizations, and nonprofits can use this information to allocate resources more effectively in these low-access areas through more targeted food access policies.
Our project specifically examines the relationship/association between residential neighborhoods/communities and nearby food access points throughout New York State. The research question guiding this paper is:

Which tract characteristics are associated with a higher probability of low access, holding other tract characteristics constant?

Our project uses census tract-level data from the USDA’s Food Access Research Atlas Data 2015 and the USDA’s Food Access Research Atlas Data 2019. The unit of observation we used is the census tract. This allowed us to analyze tract-level variation in food accessibility throughout New York State. This combined dataset includes food access indicators along with socioeconomic and demographic information. Some of the data include information on various factors. For example, vehicle access, income, race and ethnicity, housing vulnerability, SNAP participation, age, and urban classification. However, our analysis focuses on only two low food access terms, low food access at the half mile for urban and 10 mile for nonurban tracts and low food access at the 1 and 10 mile threshold.
To analyze these outcomes, we first combine the two previously mentioned data sets. Second, LASSO regression models were used to identify the most important predictors from a large set of economic, demographic, and interaction variables. Statistically significant in terms of addressing our research questions, as well as significant enough to help us provide our local analysis based on our findings. Then, selected variables were incorporated into pooled ordinary least squares (POLS), census-tract fixed-effects, year-fixed-effects, and two-way fixed-effects panel regression models.
Our project aims to contribute to an understanding of food accessibility in New York State. First, it provides a localized, census-tract-level analysis of food access in New York State. Second, our project uses machine-learning variable selection and LASSO to identify important predictors of food access inequality. Third, our project contributes practical policy insight by identifying which neighborhood characteristics are most strongly associated with low food access classifications. Our findings are interpreted as statistical associations rather than causal relationships. It is not cause and effect. Unfortunately, we do not have enough in-depth data, so our analysis will not show that. That being said, our analysis still identifies patterns and relationships between food accessibility outcomes and neighborhood characteristics. As you shall soon see, our results provide in-depth insight (not inference) into the daily lives of residents of New York state.
Ultimately, our project aims to provide insight into how low food access can affect neighborhoods throughout New York State and how policymakers and community organizations may better address food accessibility challenges in the future.

title: Exploring Socioeconomic Factors Associated with Low Food Access Tracts in New York State
text:
3.1 Data Source
The data sets used were sourced from the United States Department of Agriculture’s (USDA’s) Food Access Research Atlas for 2015 and 2019. The Food Access Research Atlas Data contains food access flags for United States census tracts using different measurement thresholds, combined with demographic and socioeconomic data from multiple data sources. The USDA defines being low access as being geographically far from a “food store”, e.g., a supermarket, supercenter, or grocery store. Both data sets use a combination of two lists of food stores to represent sources of affordable and nutritious food from 2015 and 2019, respectively.
Data used in the 2015 Atlas includes population data from the 2010 Census of the Population, urban designation provided by the 2010 Census at the block level, and data on income, vehicle availability, and SNAP participation from the 2010-14 American Community Survey (ACS). Data from the 2019 Atlas uses the same population data as 2015, with urban designations from the 2019 urbanized area geographies, and data on income, vehicle availability, and SNAP participation from the 2014-18 ACS. Both data sets are based on 2010 census-tract boundaries and contain the same classification definitions, allowing us to combine data sets into a single panel data.

title: Exploring Socioeconomic Factors Associated with Low Food Access Tracts in New York State
text:
3.2 Unit of Observation
The unit of observation for both data sets is U.S. census tracts, with each row representing one census tract. Census tracts are small, geographic subdivisions of state counties.

title: Exploring Socioeconomic Factors Associated with Low Food Access Tracts in New York State
text:
3.3 Key Variables



  



The outcome variables used are LAhalfand10 and LA1and10, which are low access flags at different measurement thresholds. A tract is deemed “low access” if at least 500 people or at least 33% of the population is greater than the measurement thresholds miles away from the nearest food store. LAhalfand10 is measured by being a half mile away for urban tracts and 10 miles for nonurban tracts, while LA1and10 is measured by being 1 mile away for urban tracts and 10 miles away for nonurban tracts.
This research focuses on socioeconomic variables, including low income tracts, poverty rate, accessibility to a personal vehicle, and population’s access to government assisted food program, SNAP. Demographic variables related to ethnicity and age are kept as control variables, while census tract and year variables will be used as fixed effects to control for time-invariant within-county characteristics and year shocks.

Demographic data that is represented as raw counts, like TractSNAP, which is the total count of housing units receiving SNAP benefits, were recalculated as the total share of population for fair comparison across tracts. title: Exploring Socioeconomic Factors Associated with Low Food Access Tracts in New York State
text:
4.1 Empirical Approach
Multiple regression models are used to examine the association between socioeconomic factors and the probability of a tract being classified as low access at the half and 10 mile threshold and the 1 and 10 mile threshold. However, the dataset has a large number of variables, many of which were highly correlated. To address this issue, Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (Lasso) regression was used for variable selection, to shrink irrelevant and highly correlated variables to zero. The Lasso model included interaction terms between year, urban classification, and all other variables to allow Lasso to select meaningful interaction terms that allow for a more flexible analysis while keeping census tract as a fixed effect to account for tract heterogeneity. After running Lasso, the variables and interaction terms selected are used for the main regression models.
\[\begin{align}
y_{it} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 Urban_{it} + \beta_2 LowIncomeTracts_{it} + \beta_3 TractHUNV_{it} + \beta_4 TractSNAP_{it} + \beta_5 \text{PovertyRate}_{it} + \delta' Z_{it} + \varepsilon_{it} \\

y_{it} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 Urban_{it} + \beta_2 LowIncomeTracts_{it} + \beta_3 TractHUNV_{it} + \beta_4 TractSNAP_{it} + \beta_5 \text{PovertyRate}_{it} + \delta' Z_{it} + \alpha_i + \varepsilon_{it} \\

y_{it} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 Urban_{it} + \beta_2 LowIncomeTracts_{it} + \beta_3 TractHUNV_{it} + \beta_4 TractSNAP_{it} + \beta_5 \text{PovertyRate}_{it} + \delta' Z_{it} + \lambda_t + \varepsilon_{it} \\

y_{it} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 Urban_{it} + \beta_2 LowIncomeTracts_{it} + \beta_3 TractHUNV_{it} + \beta_4 TractSNAP_{it} + \beta_5 \text{PovertyRate}_{it} + \delta' Z_{it} + \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \varepsilon_{it}
\end{align}\]
where \(Y_{it}\) is the outcomes LAhalfand10 and LA1and10 for census \(i\) at time \(t\), \(Z_{it}\) represents control variables, \(\alpha_i\) captures CensusTract fixed effects, \(\lambda_t\) captures Year fixed effects, and \(\varepsilon_{it}\) is the error term.
The first is a pooled ordinary least squares (POLS) model, which is used as the baseline to estimate the association between socioeconomic factors and probability of being low access across all tracts and years, reflecting a combination of cross-tract differences and within-tract changes over time. This baseline model provides estimates of the relationship between tract characteristics and being labeled food access, without accounting for unobserved heterogeneity across census tracts or time. The second is a one-way CensusTract fixed effects model, which is used to control for time-invariant characteristics within specific tracts and estimate the association between those factors and being classified as low access. The third is a one-way Year fixed effect model, used to control for factors that vary over time across all census tracts. Lastly, a two-way fixed effects model controls for both CensusTract and Year, accounting for unobserved within-tract factors and time trends/shocks.

title: Exploring Socioeconomic Factors Associated with Low Food Access Tracts in New York State
text:
4.2 Interpretations and Identification
The model results should be interpreted as estimate associations between socioeconomic factors and the probability of being classified as low access. The results are strictly descriptive, not causal, used to estimate associations and compare relationships. Positive coefficients indicate a higher probability of being labeled low access, while negative coefficients indicate a lower probability of being labeled low access, holding all other variable constant.
The POLS model reflects both differences across census tracts and changes within tracts over time, so results show the relationship between all tract’s socioeconomic factors and the probability of being low access on average. The CensusTract fixed effects model results show the relationship between socioeconomic factors and the probability of being low access within the same tract. While the Year fixed effects model results show the relationship while accounting for yearly trends and/or shocks. The two-way fixed effects model combine the two previous model, reflecting the relationship within the same tract, after removing year trends and/or shocks.

title: Exploring Patterns and Predictors of Infant Mortality Across the Globe
text:
Infant mortality is the death of a child under 1 year old, measured in deaths per 1,000 live births. For example, a rate of 9 indicates that 9 infants die for every 1,000 live births, not accounting for stillbirths or miscarriages. Infant death can be caused by several different reasons and can be caused by accidents, lack of resources, and severe living conditions (World Health Organization).
The infant mortality rate (IMR) is an important health indicator as it is a marker for a country’s overall public health, development, and social equity. Factors such as poor access to clean water, low immunization coverage, and limited economic development can have a major impact on a country’s ability to reduce infant mortality. This project aims to analyze the association between IMR and different factors, and assess their ability to predict IMR.

title: Exploring Patterns and Predictors of Infant Mortality Across the Globe
text:
Source and Scope
The main data set, “Global Health and Development (2012-2021)”, was produced by Martina Galasso by combining reliable data from the World Bank and the World Health Organization (WHO) to showcase a comprehensive overview of of global health, demographics, economic, and environmental metrics for 188 countries between 2012 and 2021. This data set included the total number of infant deaths in a year but did not include the infant mortality rate. This led me to search for another data set that provided an indicator that would allow me to calculate the infant mortality rate. The second data set, “World Bank World Development Indicators”, curated by Nicolás Ariel González Muñoz contained world development indicators from 1960 to 2022. This data set contained the birth rate, which allowed me to reverse the equations and find the infant mortality rate for every available country in the latest available year in the first data set. Both data sets were combined, resulting in a final panel data spanning 2012-2021, with each row representing one country at a specific year.

title: Exploring Patterns and Predictors of Infant Mortality Across the Globe
text:
Cleaning and Preparation
After joining both datasets, Infant_Mortality_Rate was calculated by dividing total infant deaths with total live births and multiplying by 1,000. To find the total number of live births, the Birth_Rate was divided by 1,000 and multiplied by the Total_Population. The infant mortality rate was then found by dividing the total live births with the Infant_Deaths and multiplying by 1,000. The rate was rounded to two decimal points to keep the data set from looking cluttered.
Variables with high levels of missing values were removed and remaining observations with missing values were originally estimated using the last observation carried forward with the na.locf function. The dataset was also later standardized with the scaled() for clustering.

Two-Way Fixed Effects Model
A two-way fixed effects model is used because it control for unobserved differences across countries while controlling for yearly trends and/or shocks.
\[\begin{aligned}
IMR_{it} &= \beta_0 + \mathbf{X'_{it}\beta} + \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \varepsilon_{it}
\end{aligned}\]
where the outcome is IMR in country \(i\) at time \(t\), \(\alpha_i\) captures country fixed effects, \(\lambda_t\) captures year fixed effects, and \(\varepsilon_{it}\) is the error term.









Fertility rate has the strongest association among all predictors, iplying increasing fertility by one, increases the IMR by about 6.5 deaths, holding all other factors constant. GDP per capita is the predictor with the second highest effect, with a coefficient of about 1.2. This means thatthat a 10% increase in GDP per capita is associatied with a 0.12 increase in IMR, holding everything else constant. All the other predictors are near zero indicating they have very weak association with IMR after controlling for the other predictors.

title: Exploring Patterns and Predictors of Infant Mortality Across the Globe
text:
Lasso Linear Regression
Lasso regression is used to address any multicollinearity as it performs strict variable selection, shrinking less important predictors coefficients toward zero. Country and year dummy variables are used as fixed effects to control for unobserved differences between countries and year trends and/or shocks.









Similar to the two-way fixed effects model, fertility rate has the strongest, positive coefficient, meaning increasing fertility by one, increases the IMR by about 7.8 deaths, holding all other factors constant. The lasso regression has similar results to the first model, however, log(GDP_Per_Capita)’s coefficients are reversed indicating that a 10% increase in GDP per capita is associatied with a 0.1 decrease in IMR, holding everything else constant. All other variables are near zero indicating they are very weak predictors of IMR.

title: Exploring Patterns and Predictors of Infant Mortality Across the Globe
text:
Ridge Linear Regression
Ridge regression is used to address any multicollinearity by shrinking coefficients, similar to Lasso, but instead stabilizing the shared effect among the highly correlated variables.









Compared to the lasso model, the ridge model shrinks the effect of the fertility rate to about 3.5, meaning increasing fertility by one, increases the IMR by about 3.5 deaths, holding all other factors constant. The effect of the GDP per capita is increased, showing a stronger negative effect on IMR compared to the lasso model. Sanitary expense per GDP is shrunk completely to zero, showing it does not contribute meaningfully when the other factors are considered.

If we select to show only high income countries, it appears the country that has the highest rate is Oman, however, it still only has a relatively low rate of 9.32 deaths per 1,000 live births. This highlights the great disparity between high income and lower income countries. This also shows on the map with the range between the countries. Low income countries have a high range with the lowest rate being around 17 while the highest rate is above 70. However, high income countries have a much shorter range of 9 deaths between the countries with the lowest and highest rate.

The country with the highest rate is the Central African Republic with an infant mortality rate above 70, followed by Nigeria and Chad who both have rates above 60. All the countries in the top 10 highest infant mortality rates are African and this can be explained by many factors that causes Africa to remain underdeveloped compared to other countries around the world. A major cause of this is from external factors like colonialism and the slave trade, which severely exploited many African nations and disrupted their social and economic systems. These disruptions had heavy impacts on African underdevelopment and directly contributed to the current socioeconomic environment that is causing high infant mortality rates.
It is also important to note that despite being an upper-middle income country, Equatorial Guinea still faces challenges with a high infant mortality rate. A higher income level with a high infant mortality could indicate an extreme wealth disparity and social inequality as a majority of the country could be living well below their needs while a very small portion of the population hoards an excessive amount of wealth. This is important because it shows how wealth and economic development is not the sole factor that contributes to a nation’s infant mortality rate, despite having a large impact.

Linking Access to Safe Water and Infant Mortality Rate


Code
gh3 <- gh_with_classification |> 
  mutate(Classification = factor(Classification, levels = c(
    "Low Income", "Lower-Middle Income", "Upper-Middle Income", "High Income"
  )))
ggplot(gh3,

                     y = Infant_Mortality_Rate)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = F, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(color = Classification)) +

       caption = "Source: World Bank")+

  ylab("Infant Mortality Rate") +

                              size = rel(1.5)),

    axis.title.y = element_text(size = rel(1.5)),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = rel(1.4)),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = rel(1.4)),
    legend.text = element_text(size = rel(1.3)),
    legend.title = element_text(size = rel(1.3))) +
  geom_text_repel(data = filter(gh_with_classification, Country %in% c("Palau", "Nauru")),
            aes(label = Country), 
            vjust = 0, hjust = 1.5, size = 4, force = 5) +

                  aes(label = Country), size = 4, min.segment.length = 0, hjust = 1.3) + 
  geom_text_repel(data = filter(gh_with_classification, Country %in% c("Central African Republic")),
            aes(label = Country), 
            vjust = 2, hjust = 0, size = 4, force = 5)









There is a clear negative relationship between access to safe water and infant mortality rate, as access to safe water increases, the infant mortality rate gradually decreases. However, countries with lower safe water access tend to be very scattered compared to countries with higher access to safe water. A large majority of the world’s nations have greater access to safe water; so for nations with a high safe water access percent and a high infant mortality rate, access to clean water is not a factor that would truly affect the infant mortality rate.
However, we see that the Central African Republic, the country with the highest infant mortality rate, has a severely low access to water (below 30%). This could be a major reason for the high infant mortality rate. As lack of access to safe water could cause water-born diseases to spread rapidly. Lack of safe water also leads to unhygienic living conditions, allowing disease to escalate and spread quicker. Lack of safe drinking water can also lead to dehydration for the mothers, reducing the infant’s milk supply and potentially leading to dehydration for the infant as well.

There is also a negative relationship between immunization rates and infant mortality rates, though not as steep as the relationship with access to safe water. As the percentage of people receiving immunizations increases, the infant mortality rate tends to decrease. This suggests that immunization plays a significant role in reducing preventable diseases that often contribute to infant deaths. However, there is a greater spread and variation in the infant mortality rates compared to immunization rates. There are many countries with high immunization rates who continue having a high infant mortality rate. This inconsistency indicates that immunization is a key, but not the sole driver of infant mortality.
Although Equatorial Guinea had missing data regarding safe water access, it had data regarding their immunization rates. Equatorial Guinea has a relatively low immunization rate at little over 50%. This could indicate that preventable disease could be a major factor regarding infant death. The Central African Republic also has a lower immunization rate indicating the combined circumstances of lacking safe water and low immunization could be a major reason why their infant mortality rate is so high. In regions where healthcare systems are already limited, the lack of immunization increases the risk of outbreaks of preventable disease, decreasing the infants chance at survival.
